How use(store) works

use(store) is shared state built into React. You create a store once, read it with use() while rendering, and update it from anywhere. Updates follow the same rules as useState, including transitions and rebasing, and they only re-render the components that read the store.

This page is for people who know React but not its internals. Terms like lane and record are in the glossary.

This is an experiment. It's behind the enableStore flag, and the export is unstable_createStore. In open source, it's only in the experimental build. Nothing here has shipped, and a few parts are still being decided. Those are called out where they come up, and listed in limits and decisions.

Click the button and watch the render strip under the preview. Only Count renders. App doesn't read the store, so it doesn't re-render (and there's no Provider anywhere).

The sandboxes run React 0.0.0-experimental-a3d8e745-20261101 (a3d8e745a9), the development build, without the React Compiler, with StrictMode off unless a sandbox turns it on. Every sandbox runs in your browser, offline. Press Edit to change the code and Run to try it.

The interactive explainers run the same build. The stepped ones (the queue and tearing explainers, and some sandboxes) use React's mock scheduler, so renders only happen when you step. Stepping is for illustration, and a browser doesn't schedule work that way.

The problem with Context and external stores

I don't think state that no single component owns has a good answer in concurrent React today. You can pick Context, which works with transitions but re-renders every consumer. Or you can pick an external store, which re-renders less but can't be part of a transition.

Context re-renders every component that reads it whenever the Provider's value changes, even components that only use part of the value that didn't change. A common workaround is to split Providers and memoize values.

Click Context: add one. ContextTheme re-renders even though the theme didn't change, because the Provider's value is a new object. Click Store: add one, and only StoreCount renders, because the theme is in its own store.

External stores that you read through useSyncExternalStore only re-render the components whose snapshot changed, usually with a selector per value. But React can't make an external store's update part of a transition. A change always renders synchronously, even inside startTransition. If that render suspends, the nearest Suspense boundary shows its fallback instead of keeping the current UI on screen.

The synchronous render avoids tearing. If a component reads a mutable value during a render that yields to the browser, the value can change halfway through, and one commit shows two versions of it. The tearing demo below shows all three approaches side by side.

use(store) gets both: only the components that read a store re-render, and an update inside startTransition is a transition, without tearing.

The API

There are three pieces: createStore makes a store, use(store) reads it while rendering, and store.update changes it.

import {use, unstable_createStore as createStore} from 'react';

const count = createStore(0);                 // a value
const todos = createStore([], todosReducer);  // a value and a reducer

count.update(1);                    // no reducer: a new value
count.update(n => n + 1);           // or an updater, like setState
todos.update({type: 'add', text});  // with a reducer: an action

function Count() {
  return <p>{use(count)}</p>;       // in render, even in a condition or a loop
}
  • createStore(initialValue, reducer?) makes a store. Without a reducer, update() works like a useState setter: a function is called with the current value, and anything else replaces it. With a reducer, update() passes its argument to the reducer as the action, even when it's a function.
  • The reducer is fixed when the store is created. React replays updates on top of different versions of the value when it rebases, and it does that outside any component, so the reducer can't come from a render.
  • There's no lazy initializer. The initial value is computed before anything renders.
  • store.update is bound to its store when it's created, so you can pass it around. It takes one argument. Passing a second callback argument warns in development, like setState does.
  • You can update a store from anywhere: before the first render, in an event handler, an effect, an async action, a timer, or code outside React. An update inside startTransition is a transition. Inside startGestureTransition, update() throws.
  • use(store) reads the store while rendering a function component or a custom Hook. Called outside a function component, it throws the invalid Hook call error. In useMemo, a reducer, or an effect, it gets the same warning or error as calling any Hook there.
  • There's no way to read a store outside render, so there's no store.get(). In an event handler, use the value from render or pass an updater. That's decided for the first version (DCP-21), and whether to ever add a read of the latest value is still open (see limits).
  • There are no selectors. Read granular stores instead (like a store per entity, or a store of stores), and let the React Compiler memoize what you compute from them (see what re-renders).

The mental model

A store is useReducer state that lives at the root instead of in a component. Each root that reads the store keeps its own copy of the update queue. When a render starts, the root computes the store's value for that render, with the same rules useReducer uses. Every component in the render reads that one value.

Glossary

The rest of the page uses these terms from React's internals.

Root
A React tree you create with createRoot or hydrateRoot. A page can have several.
Store
The object createStore returns. It holds the reducer, the initial value, the latest value, and the records.
Record
One root's view of a store: the updates that haven't committed, their lanes, and the components that read the store on that root.
Lane
React's priority for an update, like sync, default, or transition. A render includes some lanes and skips the rest.
Fiber
React's internal object for one component in the tree.
HostRoot
The fiber at the top of a root's tree. The states of the stores a render processed live on it, and they become each store's committed state when the root commits (DCP-17).
Work in progress
The version of the tree React is rendering, before it commits.
Base state and base queue
The state before the first skipped update, and the updates from there on. They mean the same thing as in useReducer.
Skipped lanes
The lanes of updates a render didn't apply. Components that read the store render again in those lanes.
Reader
A component subscribed to a store's record. A Suspense boundary can be one too (see Suspense).
Latest value
The value with every update applied in dispatch order. The code calls it the head. It's what a new root starts from.
Eager state
When nothing is pending on a root, the next value is computed when the update is dispatched to that root. If it didn't change, React drops the update without rendering.
Entangled
Transitions that update the same store commit together, like transitions that update the same useState.
Held update
A transition update to a store that no root reads yet. It waits on the store until the transition is done (see held updates).

What happens to one update

Step by step, from dispatch to commit:

  1. store.update(action) sends the action to every root that reads the store. Each root gives it a lane from the event's priority, the same way setState does. That's a transition lane inside startTransition and the sync lane in a click. Other events get theirs, and outside any event it's the default lane.
  2. The root queues the update on its HostRoot fiber through React's concurrent queue, and marks every component that reads the store with that lane. A render that's already running doesn't see the update. It waits for the next render.
  3. When a render starts, the HostRoot processes each store with pending updates for the render's lanes. Updates in those lanes are applied. Updates in other lanes are skipped, and the updates after a skipped one are kept, so they can be applied again in order later. That's useReducer's algorithm, run at the root instead of in each component.
  4. Every component that reads the store in this render gets that state. A store with nothing pending is read from the committed state directly. If the render skipped updates, the component gets their lanes too, so it renders again when those lanes render.
  5. On commit, the new state becomes the committed state. That's a pointer swap, and the reducer doesn't run again.

So outside hydration, two components in the same commit can't show different versions of a store. During hydration, hydrating readers render the initial value to match the server HTML, while readers rendered on the client in the same commit can show the latest value. The hydrated readers catch up in a sync render right after (see hydration).

The store itself also keeps the latest value, with every update applied in the order it was dispatched. A root that starts reading a store starts from that value, plus any held transition updates. The latest value is computed lazily, so the reducer runs about as often as it would for useReducer.

Where this lives in the code
  • packages/react/src/ReactStore.js: the store and update().
  • packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberStore.js: records, dispatch, processing at the HostRoot, commit, and dropping records.
  • useStore in ReactFiberHooks.js: reads, skipped lanes, and the subscription effect.
  • A record is split the way a Hook is. The record is the shared part, like a Hook's queue. A StoreState is the state in one version of the tree, like a Hook object. The HostRoot's state holds the StoreState of every store its render processed. DCP-17 explains why the HostRoot owns them.

Conditional reads, and what a component subscribes to

use(store) doesn't take a Hook slot, so you can read a store in a condition, in a loop, or after an early return. A component is subscribed to exactly the stores its last committed render read.

The panel below runs a Profile that always reads theme, and reads cart and user only while their checkboxes are on. Each badge reads cart. Toggle the reads, add badges, and update stores. The panel shows each store's records and subscribed components, read from the store's internals. A store that nothing reads has no record.

How subscriptions work
  • Each read goes on the component's fiber as a pair of the store's record (one per root) and the value. After the component renders, React compares the list with the previous render's. A changed value counts as an update. If nothing changed, the component bails out, like a useState update that didn't change anything.
  • A component has one internal insertion effect for all of its stores. It's only pushed when the set of stores changes. It subscribes during the commit, before layout effects run, so an update from a layout effect isn't missed. Deleting the component unsubscribes it.
  • When a component subscribes, it's marked with every lane the store has pending. That covers updates dispatched between its render and its commit.
  • When the last reader on a root unsubscribes and nothing is pending, the root drops its record in the same commit. The store doesn't keep the root alive.

A store update is a React update

A store update batches with other updates in the same event. An update inside startTransition is a transition, and a sync update is rebased over a pending transition, the same as useState.

Async actions work the same way they do with useState. Updates before and after an await commit together when the action finishes. A component whose value comes from a pending action suspends until the action is done. If no component reads the store, the HostRoot suspends on the action instead, so a reader that mounts later doesn't see the update early. There's a sandbox in patterns.

The queue, step by step

This explainer runs one component that reads a store, in real React, with the mock scheduler. Dispatch updates in different lanes, then step through the renders. The panel shows the root's record: the committed base state, the queue with each update's lane, and the updates waiting for the next render. A preview predicts each render, and a gate checks the preview against React on random sequences.

Try this. Click Transition +1, then Sync ×2. The sync update renders right away, applied to the value on screen: 1 * 2 = 2. The transition stays in the queue, with the sync update kept after it. Step, and the transition renders both in dispatch order: (1 + 1) * 2 = 4.

One thing in this explainer is React's experimental-channel behavior, not a store rule. In open source, enableDefaultTransitionIndicator is only on in experimental. With it, dispatching a transition while default updates are waiting renders those default updates at the end of the event, without a step. setState behaves the same way. Store updates don't flush differently, and stable React waits for the step.

No tearing

Every component in a render reads the same state for the store, which the HostRoot computed for that render. An update during the render goes into the concurrent queue and waits for the next render. So outside hydration, one commit never shows two versions of a store.

The demo starts a transition that renders four cells, renders two of them, changes the source, then lets React finish. Each column runs in its own frame.

  • A mutable global tears. The cells rendered after the change show the new value.
  • useSyncExternalStore doesn't tear, but the change forces a synchronous render of every cell.
  • With use(store), an update in a message event gets the default lane. The transition keeps rendering with the value it started with and commits, then the update renders.
  • With use(store), an update in a click gets the sync lane. The update renders first, and the transition starts over with the new value.

Readers that join a transition

A component that mounts while a transition is pending shows the committed value, like the components already on screen. Then it updates with the transition, in the same commit as everyone else.

When the new component reads the store, the read skips the transition's update and merges its lanes into the component's fiber. That's what useReducer does with skipped updates. There's no extra render or fixup effect.

Click Update in a transition. The transition waits for a step. Then click Mount a second reader. That's a sync render, and the new reader shows old, like the first one. Click Next commit, and both show new in one commit. A component that mounts as part of the transition itself reads the new value right away.

Held transition updates

A transition update to a store that no root reads yet is held on the store until the transition is done. That way, a component that starts reading the store in an urgent render doesn't see the update early.

Click Double it in an async transition, then Mount the first reader. The reader shows 1, because the update is held. The store panel shows it as held, with no reader yet. Click Finish the action, and the reader shows 2.

How held updates work
  • The held update waits on the store with its lane. An urgent update dispatched after it is held too, so it's rebased on top, like useReducer.
  • When a root starts reading the store, it takes the held updates into its record as if they'd been dispatched to it. It schedules their lanes on its HostRoot and entangles the transitions (DCP-20).
  • An update whose transition is done is applied to the latest value, once. That's checked at every commit and when a root starts reading the store.
  • A transition that has nothing else to render is done at the end of its event, unless it's a pending async action. So a transition that only updates an unread store doesn't hide its update.
  • A component that mounts in the same transition sees the held update.
  • With several roots, "done" is judged on the root that's committing, so a transition that's still pending on another root can be applied there early. That's how transitions already work across roots: each root commits its part on its own.
  • With several renderers on one page, like react-dom and react-art, a held update is shared by all of them. Each renderer takes it over or applies it with its own lanes.

Without a record, there's no queue to put the update in. At first the store applied it right away, and a component that mounted urgently during the transition saw it before everything else. The port of the react-concurrent-store ponyfill found that problem.

Suspense, Activity, and hydration

Suspense

If a component suspends after reading a store, an update to that store retries its Suspense boundary.

A component that suspends on mount never commits, so it never subscribes. Without help, an update wouldn't reach it, and something like use(use(store)) on a promise that never resolves would hang.

So when a component suspends, React collects the stores read by it and by the components above it, up to the nearest boundary. While the fallback shows, the boundary subscribes to those stores. A store update re-renders the boundary, which retries its children. Once they commit, they subscribe, and the boundary unsubscribes.

Profile asks for Ada, who never loads. The store panel lists the Suspense boundary as the reader. Click Show Grace instead, and the boundary retries with the new id.

What's collected, and what isn't
  • Siblings that rendered before the component that suspended aren't collected, because they can't change what it renders.
  • The collection only happens when a component suspends. A normal use(store) read does no extra work for it.
  • A store update retries only boundaries waiting on that store, and a context update retries every fallback boundary below its Provider. Children of a boundary that don't read the store aren't retried.

Activity

Readers in a hidden Activity tree update in the background at offscreen priority, and they show the latest value when they're revealed.

Click Toggle status. The visible reader renders right away, because a click is sync. The hidden reader waits, and the stepper shows pending work. Click Flush all, and the console shows the hidden reader rendering away. Reveal the panel, and the value is already there.

There's one difference from useState here, because the HostRoot owns store state. When a transition's store update commits at the root before the hidden tree renders, the hidden reader renders the committed value. useState renders the older value first, because its updates are deferred with the hidden tree.

Readers inside a tree that's being revealed read the same version as the rest of the render. Every read uses the root's lanes, not the lanes of the subtree.

Hydration

The server renders the value the store was created with, and the client hydrates with that same value. If the store changed before hydration, its readers render again with the latest value right after they hydrate. There's no mismatch and no extra API.

This sandbox renders to a string with react-dom/server, updates the store, then hydrates. The console shows the server HTML with light, the hydration render with light, and then a render with dark. There are no hydration errors.

The details
  • It's the useSyncExternalStore model, with the initial value as the server snapshot (DCP-4).
  • A hydrating reader still computes the client value. If a transition is pending, it joins it. If the client value differs from the initial value, it renders again at the sync lane after the commit (DCP-12).
  • Updates on the server aren't rendered. To server render a different value, create the store with it (for example, from data you serialize on both sides), or pass a store per request through context.
  • In development, the server warns once per store if the store was updated before the server render: A store was updated before this server render. The server renders the store's initial value, so the update isn't in the HTML, and it can't change another request's HTML either.
  • A hydrating reader doesn't throw a pending reducer error. It renders the initial value, and the error is reported at commit instead.
  • A store update isn't routed into a boundary that hasn't hydrated yet. The server HTML stays until the boundary hydrates with the initial value, and then the reader catches up.
  • Server Components can't read stores. They throw Cannot read a store from a Server Component. Passing a store as a prop to a Client Component throws too: Stores can't be passed from a Server Component to a Client Component. Create the store in a Client Component module instead.

Rules and errors

Don't update a store during render

Updating a store while rendering warns, even when the component reads that store. A store is shared, so changing it is a side effect, like updating another component.

Results copies its query into a store while it renders, and the console shows the warning. The fix is to update the store in the event that changes the query. To see the warning go away, press Edit, delete the if block, and press Run.

  • The update is rendered after the current render, the way an update to another component is. It isn't thrown away if that render suspends or is discarded.
  • An update in render that always runs causes a loop, the way updating another component in render does.
  • The useState pattern of adjusting state while rendering doesn't carry over to stores.

Warnings you won't see

Store updates never warn about unmounted components, because an update isn't tied to a component. There's also no warning about a large number of updates inside startTransition. That warning asks you to move subscriptions to React's own primitives - and a store is one.

Reducers run outside React

A store's reducer runs outside any component. Calling a Hook or reading context in it throws, and the components that read the store throw that error. Which Provider's value would a shared store see?

Normally the HostRoot runs the reducer, once per root per render. If nothing is pending on a root, it runs when the update is dispatched to that root instead, like useState's eager state. Whoever triggers it, it runs without a dispatcher.

When a read runs the reducer
  • The first read of a store on a root computes the latest value and settles held updates.
  • The first read of a record created during the render processes it then, with the render's lanes.
  • In StrictMode, React replays the reducer an extra time for readers in development, like useReducer.
  • With several roots, the eager computation can run once per root.

Reducer errors are handled like render errors

When a reducer throws, every component that reads the store throws that error while rendering, and error boundaries catch it. The update that threw is dropped, so the store recovers.

Click Add one, then Throw in the reducer. The boundary catches the error. Click its button to try again, and the count is back to its value before the update that threw. Throw in a store nothing reads shows the last case below.

  • The commit drops the update that threw, the way an error boundary drops the update queue of a useReducer it unmounts (DCP-14, amended by DCP-19).
  • If no committed error boundary logs the error, for example because the only reader is hidden, React reports it the way it reports uncaught errors (DCP-19).
  • If no root reads the store and nothing is held, an update outside a transition has no render to throw in. So store.update() throws, and the update isn't applied.
Reducer errors in held updates

A transition update to a store no root reads is held. Any update dispatched after a held one is held too, urgent or not, so it rebases on top. A reducer error in a held update is reported when the update is applied. It isn't thrown from update().

What re-renders

Which stores a component reads decides when it re-renders. A store update goes straight to its subscribed readers, without searching for them. Context, by comparison, walks the subtree looking for consumers. Each reader is marked the way a setState on it would be, which marks its path to the root, and nothing in between renders. Every reader of a changed store re-renders, and the React Compiler limits how much of each reader's output renders again.

  • An update reaches its readers past memo, PureComponent, and hidden trees without rendering the components in between.
  • There are no selectors, so a component that reads a store re-renders when any part of it changes. Split state into granular stores to narrow that down.
  • When a reader re-renders and the values an element depends on didn't change, the compiler returns the element it returned last time. A separate reconciler change, the same-element bailout, then skips reconciling it when it's the component's only child (DCP-10). It's behind its own flag, enableSameElementBailout, because it runs for every function component.

Below, the same list runs three ways. The first uses selectors through useSyncExternalStoreWithSelector, the way react-redux does. The second uses use(store) without the compiler, and the third with it. This explainer counts renders and selector calls, and flashes the components that rendered.

Click Select the next row. Selectors run for every row on every update, and only the rows whose selection changed re-render. With use(store), every Row reads the selection, so every Row re-renders. Without the compiler, every RowView re-renders with it. With the compiler, only the RowViews whose output changed render (the old and new selection). Then click Edit row 2: each row has its own store, so one Row renders in every version.

Measurements are in the benchmark report. Those are synthetic benchmarks - there's no data from a real app yet.

When rows read only one or two values

When each row reads only one or two values, a selection change with selectors runs a couple of cheap selector calls per row. With use(store), it runs every row's component instead, however cheap the compiler makes that run. The selector calls are cheaper - that comes from having no selectors, and I don't think a store-side optimization changes it.

The fix is keyed selection. Give each row its own store for the part that changes, like whether the row is selected. Then a selection updates two stores, and only those two rows re-render. A store per row does the same for row data. Both are in patterns.

Partly compiled apps and shared derived data

In a partly compiled app, readers that aren't compiled re-render their children, unless you memoize those children by hand. Expensive derived data that many components share is computed by each reader, unless you share it (see derived data).

Patterns

A store of stores

Put a store per item in a store that holds the list. Changing one item re-renders the one component that reads it. Adding an item re-renders the list, and here every item too, because the sandbox runs without the compiler or memo.

Keyed selection

Instead of every row reading the selected id, each row reads a store that says whether it's selected. Selecting a row updates the previously selected row's store and the newly selected row's store, so only those two rows re-render. It's the store version of a keyed selector, like Solid's createSelector. What re-renders covers when you need it.

The first click selects one row, so one Row renders. After that, every click renders two.

Derived data with weakMemo

Derive data in render, from the values you read. Treat store values as immutable snapshots, the way you treat useState values. Then a derivation can be cached by the identity of its arguments. Components that read the same snapshot share one result. A render that reads a different snapshot uses a different key, so it can't tear.

Five components show stats for two categories, and the console shows the stats computed twice. Add a post, and all five re-render with a new snapshot, but the stats are still computed once per category.

  • The compiler memoizes a call like f(use(a), use(b)) on both values, inline or not. It doesn't memoize a value you build across use() calls, like an array filled with push(use(a)) or built in a loop that reads stores.
  • Don't derive outside render from several stores (for example, in an update or a subscription). A value computed that way can tear with a pending transition.
  • How React should share derived data is still open. A client cache() scoped to a render is the leading option. weakMemo is the userland version the benchmarks measure.

Async actions

Updates before and after an await in an action commit together when the action finishes, the same as setState.

Click Add and save. The cart doesn't change yet, because the action is pending. Click Finish the server call, and the cart and the saved status change in one commit. The console never shows the cart updated without the status.

A store in context

Context and stores compose. Use context for which store a subtree sees, and the store for the value that changes. Readers re-render when the store changes, or when the Provider switches to a different store.

const SessionStore = createContext(null);

function Avatar() {
  const session = use(use(SessionStore)); // the context gives the store, use() reads it
  return <img src={session.avatarUrl} alt={session.name} />;
}

Differences from useState and Context

Compared with useState

By default, a store update follows the same rules as a useState update. The differences come from a store being shared and living outside the tree.

Same as useStateDifferent on purpose
Batching with other updates in the same eventA store keeps its value when its readers unmount and remount
Transitions, entanglement, and rebasingEvery component and root that reads it shares it
Async actions, flushSync, and useDeferredValueUpdating it during render warns
Suspense, and Activity except for the hidden-reader caseUpdates never warn about unmounted components
Eager state when nothing is pendingWhen nothing is pending, an update to the same value doesn't render at all, so it can render less than useState
StrictMode runs reducers twice in developmentThe reducer is fixed, and there's no lazy initializer
Error boundaries catch reducer errors thrown during renderThe server renders the initial value, and clients catch up after hydration
Readers that mount during a transition join itA hidden reader can render a transition's committed value without rendering the older one first
The update that threw is dropped and the store keeps its earlier value. When no root reads the store, update() throws instead

Because update is stable, code that detects a remount by a new setter identity needs another signal, like a useRef.

Compared with Context

A store can replace a context whose value is the same for the whole app. There's no store equivalent where Context's subtree scoping matters (the nearest Provider, a default value, shadowing, or a different value per request).

Contextuse(store)
Where the value comes fromThe nearest Provider above the componentThe store you pass to use()
What changes itThe Provider re-rendering with a new valuestore.update(), from anywhere
Who re-rendersEvery consumer of the contextOnly the components that read that store
Suspense retriesEvery boundary below the Provider showing a fallbackOnly boundaries waiting on the store
Several rootsEach root has its own ProvidersEvery root that reads the store shares it, and each root commits updates on its own schedule. Several renderers on one page each keep their own records.
DevToolsReports a context changeShows a Store Hook, and reports it as a changed Hook

Limits and decisions

These are the known limits, and the things that aren't decided yet.

  • Roots aren't kept in sync. A root that starts reading a store starts from the latest value, including updates from transitions that are still pending in another root. That's how transitions already work across roots: each root commits its part on its own. Within a root, every reader agrees.
  • Stores assume one render in progress per root. use(store) finds the root's work-in-progress tree directly. DCP-17 found nothing else that depends on there being one, but that hasn't been tested.
  • The compiler memoizes f(use(a), use(b)) on both values. It doesn't memoize a value that's still being built when use() runs, like an array filled with push(use(a)) or built in a loop over use() calls. That's because the scope that contains use() is flattened.
  • Shared derived data isn't decided. A render-scoped client cache() is the leading option. weakMemo works today.
  • The first version has no read outside render: no getSnapshot(), getState(), or subscribe() (DCP-21). Whether to ever add a read of the latest value is still open.
  • DevTools has gaps. Store values can't be edited from DevTools. const x = use(store) doesn't get a Hook name, which is also true for use(context). The Profiler does report store changes: Why did this render? lists changed Hooks by id, plus the store reads that changed.
  • The same-element bailout needs its own review. It isn't specific to stores, so it'll get its own PR (DCP-10).
  • There's no real-app data yet. The plan is to try it on a store-heavy surface and measure renders and interaction latency.
  • Not in the first version: optimistic stores, and interop with external sources and observables.
  • Independent updates to several stores already rebase together correctly. For updates that span stores, reading another store inside a reducer is a possible follow-up.
Known edge cases in reducer error reporting
  • Logged errors are matched by identity. If two stores throw the same object in one commit and a boundary logs one, it's reported once.
  • A boundary in a hidden Activity that caught the error counts as handled, but React logs it only when it's revealed. If the hidden tree is deleted first, it's never logged. Getting there needs a store update processed in an offscreen render, which in practice means an update during render.
  • Where some reducer errors should go is still open. A store has no component that owns its state, so no boundary drops its whole queue the way unmounting a useReducer does. For example, an urgent update that only throws because a pending transition was skipped can be dropped when that transition is waiting on data.

Decision index

Each design change is recorded in DECISIONS.md, with the tests that pin it. Later decisions amend or replace parts of earlier ones, and the status column says which. DCP-17 to DCP-20 don't have a status line in DECISIONS.md. They're in the code today, so they're listed as implemented. DCP-21 decides what the API leaves out, so it's listed as decided.

DecisionWhat it saysStatusEntry
DCP-1Each root keeps a lane-tagged update queue per store, with useReducer's skip and rebase rules.Accepted. Where the state lives, and the global sequence number, superseded by DCP-17.DECISIONS.md
DCP-2Readers subscribe through an internal insertion effect with no Hook slot.Accepted, amended by DCP-8.DECISIONS.md
DCP-3A read that skips updates merges their lanes into the reader's fiber, which is how a reader joins a transition.Accepted.DECISIONS.md
DCP-4The value a store is created with is what the server renders and the client hydrates with.Accepted, amended by DCP-12.DECISIONS.md
DCP-5Catching up on missed updates waits until the tree is consistent.Accepted, amended by DCP-15.DECISIONS.md
DCP-6The reducer runs as often as it does for useReducer: the latest value is computed lazily, and eager state is reused.Accepted.DECISIONS.md
DCP-7Updating a store during render warns, and the update renders after the current render.Accepted.DECISIONS.md
DCP-8One subscription effect per component, pushed only when the set of stores changes.Accepted. Amends DCP-2.DECISIONS.md
DCP-9Commits only visit the records with updates or without readers.Accepted, amended by DCP-11. The record-local commit superseded by DCP-17.DECISIONS.md
DCP-10The same-element bailout: skip reconciling a child when a component returns the same element.Accepted behind its own flag, enableSameElementBailout.DECISIONS.md
DCP-11A root drops a record after the mutation phase, once it has no readers and nothing pending.Accepted. Amends DCP-9.DECISIONS.md
DCP-12A hydrating reader computes the client value, joins pending transitions, and catches up after it hydrates.Accepted. Amends DCP-4.DECISIONS.md
DCP-13Every read in a render uses the root's lanes.Accepted. The mechanism superseded by DCP-17, which keeps the rule.DECISIONS.md
DCP-14Reducer errors throw in render, the update that threw is dropped, and when no root reads the store, update() throws.Accepted, amended by DCP-19.DECISIONS.md
DCP-15A component or boundary that subscribes is marked with every lane the store has pending.Accepted. Amends DCP-5.DECISIONS.md
DCP-16A Suspense boundary subscribes to the stores its suspended children read, so an update retries it.Accepted.DECISIONS.md
DCP-17The HostRoot owns the state of every store on its root. The HostRoot processes updates for each render, every reader in the render reads that state, and commit is a pointer swap.Implemented. Supersedes parts of DCP-1, DCP-9, and DCP-13.DECISIONS.md
DCP-18Transition updates to a store no root reads are held until the transition is done.Implemented, amended by DCP-20.DECISIONS.md
DCP-19A reducer error is reported unless a committed error boundary logs it.Implemented. Amends DCP-14.DECISIONS.md
DCP-20When a root takes over held updates, it schedules and entangles their lanes.Implemented. Amends DCP-18.DECISIONS.md
DCP-21No public read outside render in the first version. A handler uses its render's value, and read-then-write uses an updater or the reducer.Decided. A read of the latest value is still open.DECISIONS.md
